Kind of beating the dead horse on this one. I've noticed a couple issues with the way credit cards work in today's world which show me that getting into debt is the goal (i mean it was pretty obvious)

  • Most banks and credit cards will have an auto pay for the minimum, but never the statement balance. You have to go in manually and pay off the entire sum, or the auto pay will leave some money on the top. Out of all the things that should be illegal with credit cards, this is one of them. On one hand people should do their due diligence and realize this "bug", on the other hand people have way too much trust in the existing system of credit.

  • The annual interest rate is atrocious, from 19 - 32%, and can change any time. However, this is split by 12 billing cycles, so it comes down to a mere 2-3% a month instead of the full number. Incremental, slow numbers ensure people are too stupid and blind to realize they're getting robbed. When we add inflation, the interest rate goes up every year as your purchasing power goes down.

  • A lot of credit card companies realized later on that they can double dip, and charge you a card fee on top of the 30% interest rate (or whatever market rate is now). So now you have people PAYING annual fees to be in debt, and considering it a privilege. The fact that people take this as a good thing, and no amount of convincing will change their mind shows just how far down society has gone. The perks you get off the card are merely taken off the subscription fee, so essentially you're paying for your own car privileges. How people don't realize this, is beyond me. And whilst some of these cards are convenient for big companies, it makes close to no sense to have them as a consumer, especially when the fee is 450$+ per year.

  • I tell people i like to save up my money and buy cash, and leave credit for utilities and small purchase items. This ensures the credit cards are automated, and that the numbers on them are known at all times. I have gotten so much flack for doing this, because i should be "putting it all on the card". This is what the card company wants you to do, as the more you put on the card, the easier it is to completely lose track of your spending. Once that step happens, you're screwed for life. I have been berated for buying a car in cash before, as i should have just paid it off in the traditional billing cycle. However, this means i lose out on money i can save, which is going to interest. This goes to the next point, that because everything is credit, everything has exploded in price because no one "buys" an item in full anymore.

  • Because everything revolves around debt and credit, nothing can ever be bought at normal price. A car which used to cost 15 or 20K now costs 35K. A medical bill which used to cost 100$, now costs thousands. Even if you don't want to join the system, the system will find a way to force itself down your throat. I tried asking someone how income works if the company is in debt, and your income comes from credit? Essentially your income isn't backed by anything tangible, just the promise that the company wont go bankrupt. Multiply this over multiple avenues, and you essentially have debt being used to create debt being used to create even more debt. It becomes its own self sustaining debt currency, as nothing is bought with tangible assets anymore. This same reasoning is why a house which cost 75,000 in the 70s, now costs 600,000.

  • Because everything is debt and credit based, everything is a subscription. Your mortgage and house is essentially a subscription too. Don't pay mortgage? Evicted. Pay of mortgage? Well now pay property tax. Then you have HOA fees on top of that, maintenance, etc. I can't think of a single product which hasn't converted into some kind of subscription service, be it Microsoft or Apple. Same with cars, medical bills, tuition. None of these will ever get repayed in your lifetime depending on their severity, so essentially your entire life is one big pay to play subscription service.

  • The credit score promotes the idea that someone who has 100,000 in debt making minimum payments buying a new car every 2 years has a better grasp on finances and how to manage money than someone who saves up for items and buys them in cash.

No, he's talking about when you get 2-3% of your purchase amounts back from your credit card company every month. /u/ImOnAVoatSon explained it pretty well: Credit card companies charge retailers a percentage of every transaction for their 'service.'

So 20 years ago, let's say you buy a snickers bar for $1 with your Visa card. The payment processor (the people who facilitate access to Visa, Mastercard, etc.) charges the retailer who sold you the snickers bar 5%, or 5 cents. You pay your $1 credit card bill. The retailer, who paid 50 cents wholesale for that snickers, profits 45 cents after his payment processor fee.

These days, since so many credit cards compete with one another with varying levels of 'cash back,' let's say you buy that same $1 snickers bar with your Chase Sapphire Reserve card, which gives you 2.5% back on all your purchases. When you pay your bill, you're only paying 97.5 cents for that candy bar. What a deal, right? Except now, the payment process is charging the retailer 8% to cover that cash back you're getting (and pocketing an extra .5% for themselves.) So the payment processor gets 8 cents from the retailer. The retailer's profit margin is now just 42 cents.

The next time you go to the store, you see that the snickers bar is priced at $1.08, as the retailer tries to recover his profit margin. Credit card companies continue to compete with better points & cashback incentives, and in turn raise fees for retailers, who in turn raise prices. The credit card companies aren't really doing anything more for us than they were 20 years ago, but they've figured out a way to extract more money from both consumers & businesses.
